phase1.intro:
enum is Java's way of saying "this variable can only ever be one of a fixed, known set of values" — and the compiler actually enforces that.

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: How does a basic enum work?
dialogue: `enum Day { MONDAY, TUESDAY, ... }` declares seven constants, and a `Day` variable can genuinely never hold anything else — no typos, no invalid values slipping through.

Every enum comes with a few methods for free: `.values()` hands back every constant in order, `.ordinal()` gives you each one's position (0-indexed), and `Day.valueOf("MONDAY")` parses a String back into the matching constant.

stickyNote.definition: enum Day { MONDAY, ... } restricts a variable to a fixed set of constants. .values(), .ordinal(), and .valueOf() come free.

topics.buttonText: Can an enum constant carry its own data?
dialogue: Enums aren't limited to bare names — look at `Planet`: [[key:each constant can carry its own data and even its own constructor call]], `MERCURY(3.30e23, 2.44e6)` runs Planet's constructor with those exact values, once per constant, when the enum first loads.

Enums can have completely ordinary methods too, like `Status.isFinished()` — [[key:an enum is genuinely a class under the hood]], just one where the compiler already knows every possible instance in advance.

stickyNote.flavor: 🪐 each constant can carry its own fields
stickyNote.definition: Enum constants can carry constructor arguments (MERCURY(3.30e23, 2.44e6)) and the enum can have ordinary methods — it's a real class under the hood.

topics.buttonText: Are there limits to what an enum can do?
dialogue: [[warn:An enum can't extend any other class]] — it already implicitly extends `java.lang.Enum`, and Java only allows single inheritance, so that slot's taken. It can still implement interfaces, though.

stickyNote.flavor: 🚫 already extends Enum, that slot's taken
stickyNote.definition: An enum implicitly extends java.lang.Enum, so it can't extend anything else — but it can still implement interfaces.

phase1.openingDialogue: enum locks a variable to a fixed, known set of values — and each constant can carry its own data and methods. 🎲

phase2.errorMessage:
Test.java:9: error: constant string required
            case Red:  // Wrong case — should be RED
                 ^
1 error
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:Enum constants inside a switch have to match exactly, and they're case-sensitive]] — `Red` and `RED` are not the same identifier. `Color.RED` is spelled in all caps, by convention, and the switch case has to use that exact spelling.

[[key:Inside a switch on an enum, you write just the constant name, no enum prefix needed]] — `case RED:`, not `case Color.RED:` or `case Red:`. The fix here is simply capitalizing it correctly: `case RED:`.

mcq.question:
What does calling .values() on an enum return?

A) A single random constant
B) An array containing every constant declared in the enum, in order
C) The number of constants declared
D) A String representation of the enum's name

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create an enum OrderStatus with values:
• NEW, PROCESSING, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED

Add methods:
• isActive() — returns true for NEW, PROCESSING, SHIPPED (not delivered or cancelled)
• getDescription() — returns a description for each status

In main, iterate through all statuses and print their description and active status.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: because Java guarantees each enum constant is created exactly once, ever, enums are actually a well-known technique for implementing the Singleton design pattern safely — it's a recommendation that comes up often in Java best-practice writing, since a plain enum with one constant gets you serialization-safety and thread-safety that hand-written singletons often get wrong.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thing before you fix your set of values~
